pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Animal Homes, ages 5–7 — animals make or find many different kinds of home (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge) and these shelters protect the animal and its babies. Second-most-central young topic (0.134), building directly on 'Animals Everywhere'.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS1 Y2 'Living things and their habitats' — how habitats provide for the basic needs of animals (shelter); links to the curriculum 'Habitats & Basic Needs' topic.
• Standards — US: NGSS K-ESS3-1 (needs of organisms and the places they live) and 1-LS1-1 (animals use external parts / behaviours to help them survive and meet their needs — building, digging, spinning a home).
• Operational details: teach the distinction MAKE vs FIND (a bird builds a nest and a beaver builds a lodge, but a hermit crab FINDS an empty shell); connect every home to its JOB — shelter from weather/predators and a safe place for young; match common animals to their homes; use a cutaway view so children see the animal (and babies) INSIDE, which anchors 'a home keeps them safe' rather than 'a home is just where it sits'.
• Checkpoint: [Tier A] names ≥4 home types (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), explains that homes give shelter and keep babies safe, and correctly matches common animals to their homes.
bestPractices: Tie every home to its PURPOSE (shelter from cold/rain, hiding from predators, a safe nursery for young) so 'home' means protection, not just a location — a cutaway showing the animal and its babies tucked inside makes this concrete.

Draw the MAKE-vs-FIND contrast explicitly: some animals build their home (nest, web, hive, lodge, burrow) and some find or borrow one (hermit crab in a shell, animals sheltering in a hollow log) — this adds a satisfying sorting dimension for 5–7.
Use matching as the core activity (animal ↔ home) because the KS1 evidence is 'matches common animals to their homes'; give immediate feedback so a wrong match is a gentle, correctable surprise.
Cover a spread of home types across land, water and air to reinforce the just-learned 'animals everywhere' idea (underground burrow, treetop nest, underwater lodge, garden web).
Keep human houses as a relatable bridge but distinguish them — animals build with what nature provides (mud, twigs, wax, silk), no shops or tools.
keyRepresentations: Cutaway home illustrations (a burrow underground, a nest in a tree, a hive's cells, a lodge in water) showing the animal and its young sheltered inside.
An animal↔home matching board (bird→nest, rabbit→burrow, bee→hive, spider→web, hermit crab→shell, fox→den, beaver→lodge).
A MAKE / FIND sort (built homes vs found/borrowed homes).
Home→material pairings (nest = twigs & grass, hive = wax, web = silk, lodge = sticks & mud) to show animals build from nature.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking every animal builds its own home — missing that some FIND or borrow one (the hermit crab uses a cast-off shell; some animals shelter in existing holes).
Believing a home is just 'where the animal sits/lives', not grasping its job as protection and a safe place for babies.
Assuming animals build like people do (with tools or bought materials) rather than from natural materials (mud, twigs, wax, silk).
Over-generalising one home type ('all animals live in nests') to every animal.
Confusing a whole HABITAT (the woodland, the pond) with the animal's specific HOME (its nest, its burrow) within that habitat.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7 (Animal Homes): children learn that animals MAKE or FIND many kinds of home (nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), that each home has a JOB — shelter from weather and predators and a safe place for young — and can match common animals to their homes. The central activity is an active animal↔home match where a correct match reveals the animal and its babies sheltered inside, plus a BUILT-vs-FOUND sort. Supporting scaffolds (tap-to-reveal cutaway scenes and a short recognition check) and a hands-on 'gather natural materials' step are included to make 'home = protection' concrete and to distinguish the specific home from the wider habitat.

activities.title: Take each animal home (match and peek inside)
feedback: On a correct match: open a cutaway revealing the animal sheltered inside, with its young where that home is used for raising them, plus a short cue such as 'keeps them warm' or 'keeps them hidden'.
On a wrong match: a gentle nudge — the animal politely won't fit there — prompting a rethink rather than marking it simply 'wrong'.
Prompt the child to name the home's job after each match ('What does this home do for the animal?').
activities.rationale: Active matching with immediate, correctable feedback targets the stated KS1 evidence ('matches common animals to their homes'), and revealing sheltered young on a correct match makes the protection purpose something the child causes and sees rather than only reads.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of animals, including shelter.
Animals use external parts and behaviours (building, digging, spinning) to help them survive and meet their needs, including shelter for themselves and their young.

Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
learnerActions: Look at a scene with several places — a tree, a grassy bank, a pond, a garden corner and a seashore rock pool — and a row of animals waiting to go home.

Match each animal to its home: bird→nest (in the tree), rabbit→burrow (in the grassy bank), bee→hive (in a hollow in the tree), spider→web (in the garden corner), hermit crab→shell (in the seashore rock pool), fox→den (in the bank), beaver→lodge (in the pond).

On a correct match, look inside the opened/cutaway home to see how it protects the animal (eggs warm in the nest, kits deep in the burrow, cubs in the den, bee grubs in the wax cells). Not every home holds babies: the hermit crab's shell protects its soft body, and a spider's web mainly catches food, with eggs kept in a silk egg sac.
Say out loud what the home is for — e.g. 'it keeps them warm', 'it hides them from danger'.
When a match is wrong, notice the animal won't fit and try a different home.
activities.intendedInsight: A home is not just where an animal sits — it is shelter that protects the animal, and many homes also keep babies safe; different animals have different homes.

activities.title: Built or found? (a sorting surprise)
feedback: Confirm a correct sort and name the reason ('the bird made this', 'the crab found this one, it didn't build the shell').
For a mis-sort, revisit how that home comes to be (who made it) before re-sorting.
activities.rationale: An explicit MAKE-vs-FIND contrast directly addresses the common misconceptions that every animal builds its own home and that people make animals' homes, while adding a satisfying sorting dimension suited to this age.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
Animals use external parts and behaviours (building, digging, spinning) to help them survive and meet their needs, including shelter for themselves and their young.
learnerActions: Sort the homes into two groups: ones the animal BUILT (nest, web, hive — bees build the wax comb, often inside a hollow they found — lodge, burrow) and ones it FOUND or borrowed (the hermit crab's empty shell; an animal sheltering in a hollow log).
Explain for one or two examples how it was made or found — a bird gathers twigs and grass; a hermit crab backs into an empty shell left behind by a sea snail.
Talk about the surprise that not every animal makes its own home.
activities.intendedInsight: Some animals build their home and some find or borrow one — so 'animals have homes' does not mean 'every animal builds a nest'.

activities.title: Explore the habitat scene (tap to peek inside)
feedback: Each tap reveals the home and a brief purpose cue; invite the child to name the home type before or after revealing it.
activities.rationale: A calm tap-to-reveal scene reliably introduces several home types and the 'safe inside' idea across land, water and high places, reinforcing the just-learned 'animals everywhere' idea. It is a scaffold for exposure; it does not require the child to commit to a match, so pair it with an active matching task.
sourceClaims: KS1 pupils should describe how different habitats provide for the basic needs of animals, including shelter.
learnerActions: Explore a habitat picture spanning land, water and high places (underground burrow, treetop nest, beaver lodge in a pond with an underwater entrance and a dry room above the water, garden web).
Tap a place — the tree, the ground, the pond — to open a cutaway of the home with the animal and its young inside.
Read or hear a one-line 'what it's for' and point to where the babies are kept safe.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals live in homes all around us — underground, up in trees and bushes, and in and beside water — and each cutaway shows the animal sheltered inside.

activities.title: Build like an animal does (natural materials)
feedback: Praise correct home→material pairings; if a child names a shop-bought material, point back to what the animal could actually find in nature.
activities.rationale: Pairing each home with its natural material confronts the pedagogy-identified misconception that animals build like people do with tools or purchased materials, and a hands-on gathering step makes the idea tangible. This materials-vs-shops point is a research-informed proposal drawn from the pedagogy guidance rather than a verified source claim.
learnerActions: Gather pretend or real natural materials to make a simple home — twigs and grass for a nest, sticks and mud for a lodge.
Name the material for each home: nest = twigs & grass, hive = wax, web = silk, lodge = sticks & mud.
Notice that animals build from what nature provides — no shops, no bought tools.
activities.intendedInsight: Animals build with natural materials they find, not with tools or materials bought from shops the way people do.

activities.title: Home vs whole place, and who makes it (talk check)
feedback: Target answer: the nest is for shelter and protection — a safe place to lay eggs and keep chicks warm and hidden from predators and weather; the bird builds it from twigs, grass and moss, and people do not make it.

If the child describes the bird sleeping there all year with rooms/furniture, note that many nests are mainly for eggs and chicks and adults often don't 'live' there once the young fledge; focus on protection of the young.
If the child says a person builds or gives the nest, revisit a bird gathering material and building it itself.
If the child names the forest or garden as the home, distinguish the specific shelter (nest) from the wider place.
activities.rationale: Asking FUNCTION and MAKER together separates a child who pictures a nest as a little human house from one who understands a home as protection the animal makes or finds, and it surfaces the habitat-vs-home confusion.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly assume all animals build nests or that a home is merely a location rather than protective shelter; contrasting built vs found homes and showing young sheltered inside addresses this.
learnerActions: Answer: 'A bird's nest and your house are both called homes. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?'

Answer follow-ups: Why do many birds build a nest when they lay eggs? Does a bird stay in its nest all day and night the way you stay in your house? Where is a rabbit's home — up a tree or under the ground, and why? Did the hermit crab build its shell or find it?
Point to the specific home (the nest) versus the wider place the animal lives in (the forest, the garden).
activities.intendedInsight: A home is the specific shelter that protects the animal and its young, which the animal builds or finds itself — different from the whole habitat it lives in.

constraints: Checkpoint (Tier A): the child names ≥4 home types (from nest, burrow, hive, web, shell, den, lodge), explains that homes give shelter and keep babies safe, and correctly matches common animals to their homes.
Tie every home to its purpose (shelter from cold/rain, hiding from predators, a safe nursery) so 'home' means protection, not merely a location.
Cover a spread of home types across land, water and high places (trees, bushes), including homes of flying animals, to reinforce that animals live everywhere.
Keep human houses only as a relatable bridge, and distinguish them: animals build from natural materials (mud, twigs, wax, silk), not shop-bought materials or tools.

A tap-to-reveal scene can teach and check recognition of home types, but recognition alone does not require the child to independently commit to and self-correct a match; include an active matching task for that production.
A peek-inside 3D den can serve as a novelty reward, but spatial navigation is not the learning goal here; the goal is matching and purpose.

Open in-role dialogue is a weaker fit for this factual matching content with 5–7s and can drift; prefer the matching/sorting tasks, using the focused spoken questions above as a check. This is a suitability judgement for this topic, not a claim that dialogue cannot teach.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
All three cited sources are marked verified:false in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.
The natural-materials-vs-shops point in the 'Build like an animal does' activity derives from pedagogy.commonMisconceptions, not from a source claim, so its sourceClaims is []; keep it as a proposal.

The original source rated conversation 'poor' and asserted 3D 'adds nothing' / dialogue 'adds little'; these are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to narrowly scoped suitability notes with stated limits.
The claim that a static/tap-reveal scene does not elicit active match-and-check is treated as a narrow recognition-vs-production affordance, not a claim that such scenes cannot teach.

Treating 'web' and 'shell' as protective homes for young is an age-appropriate simplification inherited from the original; it is not biologically precise (webs are chiefly prey traps; spiders guard eggs in egg sacs) and should be refined if later accuracy is needed.

probeDeeper: Why do birds need a nest when they lay their eggs?
Does a bird stay in its nest all day and night the way you stay in your house?
Where is a rabbit's home — up a tree or under the ground? Why there?
A hermit crab uses an empty shell as its home — did it build that shell, or find it?
assess.correctAnswer: The nest is for shelter and protection — a safe place to lay eggs and keep the chicks warm and hidden from predators and weather. The bird itself builds the nest, gathering twigs, grass and moss; people do not make it for the bird.

errorPatterns.pattern: A nest is a human-style house — the bird lives there all the time with its things, like we live in our house.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Many nests are only for eggs and chicks; adult birds often don't 'live' in them once the young fledge. Focus on protection of eggs and babies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the bird sleeping there every night year-round, or gives it rooms/furniture; treats it as a residence rather than a shelter for raising young.

errorPatterns.pattern: People make animals' homes for them.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Watch a bird gathering material and building; the animal makes or finds its own home (hermit crab finds a shell, rabbit digs a burrow).
errorPatterns.distractor: A person builds the nest for the bird.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says a person builds the nest, or that the bird was 'given' its home.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses the home with the whole habitat — 'the bird's home is the forest'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the specific shelter (the nest) from the wider place the animal lives in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the wider place (forest, garden) rather than the specific shelter.

responseLevels.gap: Treats a nest as a human-style house or thinks people make it; no sense of shelter/protection.
responseLevels.full: Explains the home shelters and protects the animal and its young, and that the animal builds or finds it itself, giving an example (nest, burrow, shell).
responseLevels.partial: Names several homes and matches animals to them, but explains 'home' as just 'where it lives' without the protection function, or is unsure who makes it.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bird's nest and your house are both called 'homes'. What is a nest FOR — what does it do for the bird? And who makes a bird's nest?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Asking the FUNCTION and the MAKER together separates a child who pictures a nest as a little human house (where the bird 'lives', furnished, built by people) from one who understands a home as protection the animal makes or finds itself. The 'who makes it' tier catches the very common 'people build it' idea.
